Katsitsaronkwas Shyann White, Mohawk du: Katsitsaronkwas Shyann White, a Mohawk from the territory of Kahnawà:ke, says we need more Indigenous people in public administration and governance. The growing number of Indigenous-led initiatives and organizations is an important step in the fight against systemic racism.
Elle fait partie des diplômés de McGill: She is among the McGill graduates honoured at the 11th annual scarf ceremony, organized by the Indigenous Peoples’ House. This year, the scarf ceremony was held virtually, with 60 graduates of Indigenous background.
Mme White a terminé le programme d’admin: Ms. White completed the public administration and governance program with distinction, on the Dean’s Honour List and with an Indspire Award. She did the program full-time while also working full-time as a receptionist for the Mohawk Council of Kahnawà:ke.
« Je voulais un meilleur avenir », dit-e: “I wanted a better future,” she says. The public administration and governance program seemed well balanced to her, and it was the “Indigenous cohort” that cemented her decision. “I met people from different backgrounds and different nations, and it was comforting. I didn’t feel out of place, and I felt like I belonged here.”Seven years had passed since she had done secretarial training, and the online format fit her work and family life, as she is a mother of three. The connection with fellow Indigenous students reminded her of high school, when she took the bus across the Mercier Bridge to Montréal to get to class. “There was only one person I knew on the bus, and I felt anxious until I met other Indigenous students.”
Mme White est fière d’avoir intégré un n: Ms. White is proud to have started a new job last week, as administrative assistant to the director of Kateri Memorial Hospital. She says the program helped her a great deal in her career, and that she appreciated the involvement of postsecondary education advocates who understand the benefits of “Indigenous education, the Indigenous way.”
Elle nous confie que l’année a été diffi: She tells us the year was difficult and that COVID-19 was only one of the challenges. “Luckily, our program was already online; we just kept up the pace, and we could always communicate with one another,” says Ms. White. “I can give back to my community in a way that is so valuable and enriching.”
<strong>Prendre les devants, selon les p: Taking the lead, guided by Indigenous perspectives
Tatiana Lamoureux Gauvin est chargée de: Tatiana Lamoureux Gauvin is a lecturer in the public administration and governance program at McGill University’s Desautels Faculty of Management. “Teaching intercultural communication to an Indigenous cohort was an eye-opening experience,” she says.
Le fait d’offrir le programme entièremen: Offering the program entirely online allowed more students to take part, whether they live in the James Bay region or in Haida Gwaii, British Columbia. The cohort gave her a greater appreciation of the diversity of Indigenous nations in Canada. “Through this course, I discovered the richness and variety of cultural differences within the different Indigenous communities themselves, and within subcultures,” says Ms. Gauvin. “I learn from every story a student shares.”
Patrika McEvoy termine son dernier cours: Patrika McEvoy is finishing her last course this week. She attended classes by videoconference from Haida Gwaii. In her view, the Nation Rebuilding program is an important theme in today’s public administration and governance sector. It is work she knows well, as a councillor with the Old Masset council of the Haida Nation. “Reconciliation is hard work, and we can develop solutions to the problems they created with the genocide.”“If we can implement the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in my lifetime, that will be half the battle,” says Ms. McEvoy. Reconciliation necessarily involves creating a space for exchange where the Indigenous point of view takes precedence.
« En tant que femme autochtone, j’ai app: “As an Indigenous woman, I’ve learned to bring our reality into our studies whenever the opportunity arises,” she continues. “We can see it when the TRC’s recommendations are implemented in institutions, because then we have the right to speak and tell our own stories. It’s an uncomfortable conversation, but one we have to have every chance we get.”
Teiawenniserate Jeremy Tomlinson, de Kan: Teiawenniserate Jeremy Tomlinson, from Kanehsatà:ke, agrees. “There’s always a noticeable difference when we, as Indigenous people, make up the majority in a group. There’s more comfort,” he says. “It’s hard to explain, but in our daily lives, when we work or take part in other activities within the colonial system, we often have defence mechanisms in place. It’s as if, having dealt with so much discrimination and racism, we’ve come to expect the upsetting questions and comments.”“I can speak to the case of one professor in particular: Kit Malo. She was very open and truly mediated a forum that allowed me to feel comfortable sharing my experience as part of the learning activities,” says Mr. Tomlinson.
Selon Kit Malo, la valorisation des expé: According to Kit Malo, valuing the lived experiences and learning of Indigenous people is essential, particularly in courses with Indigenous content or awareness-raising courses. She is a lecturer in organizational behaviour.Ms. Malo would like resources to be made available to increase the number of Indigenous speakers in all faculties and schools. “I’ve thought about this as a white person who received a colonial education, and my perspective is going to reinforce a lot of the things I think we need to unlearn,” she says.The professor uses a co-learning approach, which helps her navigate themes that lend themselves naturally to the expression of Indigenous voices.
« Il s’agit d’un espace où je pouvais pa: “It’s a space where I could talk about things from a perspective that matters deeply to me, and be with a group of people who want to have these conversations and approach them through their lived experience, but also their wisdom, their intelligence and their perspective. It’s incredibly enriching,” she says.In her view, this reinforced an approach that suits her teaching style, which involves examining organizational behaviour from a critical standpoint. “And talking about it in a way that is as anti-racist and anti-oppressive as possible,” she adds. “One of the questions I ask myself about non-Indigenous teachers, myself included, is how consistently we are learning, building connections to understand, absorbing and listening to Indigenous cultures and systemic issues.”
Carole Brazeau, directrice du programme: Carole Brazeau, director of the Indigenous Initiatives program in the Office of the Principal and Vice-Chancellor, says 451 Indigenous students are currently enrolled at McGill. The university had 39,736 students in 2020.
Ce petit nombre ne surprend pas M. Tomli: Mr. Tomlinson is not surprised by this small number. “More and more, our fellow community members feel uncomfortable in these institutions, because they face discrimination and racism every day. The burden of ‘reconciliation’ now rests on the shoulders of our people, because Indigenous people are still seen as the problem when it comes to improving relations,” he says.A 2019 profile of Indigenous postsecondary students shows a conscious attempt to increase Indigenous content. But there is a difference between “inserting content” and incorporating Indigenous worldviews on power sharing and communication, which are highly relevant to teaching, learning and group discussions.
« Ce n’est pas facile à naviguer », esti: “It’s not easy to navigate,” says Mr. Tomlinson. “You have to strike a balance between ‘modern’ education and the promotion and revitalization of Indigenous cultural knowledge and languages.”
Cela se reflète dans son propre parcours: That is reflected in his own path. He left his studies, choosing instead to devote himself to learning and teaching his language, Kanien’kéha.Increasing Indigenous participation is one thing; having the emotional intelligence and communication skills to create safer spaces is another.
Pour l’enseignante Tatiana Lamoureux Gau: For instructor Tatiana Lamoureux Gauvin, this is an essential element: “Creating safe spaces isn’t only about creating spaces where students feel comfortable speaking, but also about establishing secure spaces that are respectful.”
La Dre Carmen Sicilia est directrice des: Dr. Carmen Sicilia is director of Indigenous relations at McGill University’s School of Continuing Studies. She reflects on the lessons learned from the program’s first Indigenous cohort.“One lesson is that some of these conversations are sometimes hard to handle for non-Indigenous lecturers and professors,” she says. “Difficult conversations can bring up emotions and trauma for students. We learned that we need to provide support – better support and more support at the same time – to teachers and students.”
La médiation tenant compte des traumatis: Trauma-informed mediation was a need raised by an Indigenous student in the program, along with a request that more Indigenous leaders take part in these conversations.
« C’est vraiment important, dit Mme Sici: “It’s really important,” says Ms. Sicilia. “They need to be supported not only in the classroom, but also when they leave the classroom. We have to be conscientious and aware, and be able to create a secure space. When they leave, they still feel safe and know they can turn to someone to talk.”
L’une des choses sur lesquelles travaill: One of the things Ms. Sicilia is working on is inviting Elders from various communities across Canada so they can provide part-time support to students and teachers. She hopes this initiative can be implemented beyond this particular program.
Après la cérémonie du foulard, la Facult: After the scarf ceremony, the School of Continuing Studies held a virtual convocation in this pandemic year. In all, 60 Indigenous students graduated, including 3 in public administration and governance.
La célébration a rendu hommage aux diplô: The celebration honoured the graduates and took care to honour the memory of the children of the residential school on the territory of Tk’emlúps te Secwe̓pemc.
En tant que diplômée autochtone, j’ai ét: As an Indigenous graduate, I was invited to speak at the graduation ceremony. I began by expressing my gratitude to my own mother, who began her schooling in one of those “schools” and who, even so, still values education for what it can give us.
Les leçons apprises au sein de notre coh: The lessons learned within our Indigenous cohort showed how hard the work of dismantling systemic racism is, and the beauty of what can happen. Creating places for Indigenous students is one part of it, but we also have to make sure there is no room left for racism in classrooms.
